 Sanders donates $1M to El-Sayed campaign in Michigan Senate race 
 By Calvin Cutler Published : Oct. 23, 2026 at 6:12 PM EDT | Updated : 6 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is pouring $1 million into Michigan’s hotly contested U.S. Senate race, a move that highlights the role of money and power in politics as control of the Senate hangs on the outcome of the midterm election.
 The Michigan race pits Republican Mike Rogers against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
 This week, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, signaled it was prepared to spend up to $9 million on behalf of Rogers.
 The New York Times reports that Sanders, who has been at the heart of a fight with AIPAC and its influence in politics, responded by donating $1 million to a pro-El-Sayed political action committee to boost him in the final days of the campaign.
 For context, $1 million is more money than Republican Phil Scott or progressive Democrat Amanda Janoo has raised or spent in the competitive Vermont governor’s race.
 The money comes out of Sanders’ campaign war chest. Sanders currently has more than $22 million left over from his Senate and two unsuccessful presidential runs. Under campaign finance rules, he can donate any amount to political organizations that support other political candidates.
 Sanders defended his spending and criticized AIPAC and the war in Iran.
 “AIPAC’s agenda is not the agenda of the American people. They want U.S. taxpayers to continue supporting the genocidal government of Netanyahu in Israel. They want a continuation of the horrific war in Iran, which has raised prices in the United States and cost us the lives of 19 U.S. service members. We have got to stand up to a PAC and their agenda,” said Sanders, I-Vermont.
 Vermont’s senior senator has long bemoaned the presence of big money in politics. But political analysts I spoke with say this cash infusion signifies the high stakes of this race.
 “He has, as you well know, run constantly critical of the 1% who he says have wielded a disproportionate influence on politics in America, and yet he is weighing in with a major campaign contribution. His defense would be, you have to fight fire with fire,” said Matt Dickinson, a political science professor at Middlebury College.
 Dickinson added the race in Michigan is an opportunity for progressives like Sanders and El-Sayed to show that their progressive message can win in purple states.
 Sanders will spend this weekend in Michigan campaigning for El-Sayed.
